## Can two surveys inform the same environmental response?

Suppose one bird survey records whether a species was detected, while another
records its count during a fixed observation period. Both might tell us about
the response to woodland cover, but a binary observation is not a count.
`mgcv::gfam()` fits one model in which each row has its own response family.
The new gratia support provides response draws and diagnostics that respect
that membership. This differs from a delta model: here the two sources supply
separate observations, rather than occurrence and positive abundance being
parts of a single response distribution.

We simulate fixed-effort surveys at independent sites. The log odds of
detection and the log expected count have different intercepts but share the
same smooth response to woodland cover. Sharing the curve assumes that a
change in cover has the same effect on log odds and log expected count. We
compare this assumption with survey-specific curves below.

The code needs mgcv and gratia, and uses dplyr and ggplot2 for presentation.
All are gratia dependencies. The example has 600 observations and uses 200
coefficient draws; increase the latter for final interval estimates.

```{r packages}
library("gratia")
load_mgcv()
library("dplyr")
library("ggplot2")
```

```{r surveys}
set.seed(241)
survey <- data.frame(
  woodland = runif(600),
  source = factor(rep(c("Detection", "Count"), each = 300),
    levels = c("Detection", "Count"))
)
survey$family_id <- as.integer(survey$source)
habitat <- function(x) 1.8 * sin(pi * x) - 0.8 * x
eta <- ifelse(survey$source == "Detection", -1.3, 0.2) +
  habitat(survey$woodland)
survey$observed <- ifelse(survey$source == "Detection",
  rbinom(600, size = 1, prob = plogis(eta)),
  rpois(600, lambda = exp(eta)))
ggplot(survey, aes(woodland, observed)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.25) +
  facet_wrap(~ source, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Proportion of woodland", y = "Survey response")
```

The binary panel contains only zero and one. The count panel has a wider range
and variance that grows with the mean. A binomial family with one trial and a
Poisson family are appropriate for the simulated protocols. For real counts,
extra variation may require `nb()` instead of Poisson; residual checks help
assess that choice.

## Share the smooth, retain different intercepts and links

The two-column response supplies the observation and its position in the family
list. Family 1 is binomial and family 2 is Poisson. The factor `source` supplies
different intercepts. A single `s(woodland)` supplies the shared effect on both
linear predictors, and REML estimates its smoothness.

```{r fit}
joint <- gam(cbind(observed, family_id) ~ source + s(woodland, k = 10),
  data = survey, family = gfam(list(binomial(), poisson())), method = "REML")
draw(joint, parametric = FALSE)
```

A positive smooth contribution multiplies the expected count by `exp(effect)`
and multiplies detection odds by the same quantity. It does not add the same
amount to the detection probability and count. The fitted smooth rises toward
intermediate cover and then declines, consistent with the generating response.
Its centering constraint sets the reference for the partial effect. The
different intercepts determine the absolute levels.

The [mgcv grouped-family documentation](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/mgcv/html/gfam.html)
explains the response encoding and sharing of terms. This example replaces
its generic simulation with two explicitly described survey protocols.

Sharing a smooth can improve precision if its assumption is reasonable. A model
with different smooths provides a useful comparison when the surveys have enough
information to estimate them:

```{r different-responses}
separate <- gam(cbind(observed, family_id) ~ source +
    s(woodland, by = source, k = 10),
  data = survey, family = gfam(list(binomial(), poisson())), method = "REML")
draw(separate, parametric = FALSE)
```

Compare the shapes and their uncertainty, particularly at the ends of the cover
range. The binary survey contains less information about the curve than the
count survey, so its wider intervals leave more uncertainty about its shape.
The similar fitted shapes support sharing in this simulation. For your own
surveys, use separate smooths if the protocols imply different responses to
cover, and include offsets when survey effort varies.

## Predict the appropriate quantity for each survey

Prediction rows must identify their distribution. This matters even if their
covariates are identical. We generate the same cover grid for both protocols
and pass `family_index` explicitly. Response-scale `fitted_samples()` applies
each row's inverse link to every shared coefficient draw.

```{r predictions}
grid <- expand.grid(woodland = seq(0, 1, length.out = 80),
  source = levels(survey$source))
grid$source <- factor(grid$source, levels = levels(survey$source))
index <- as.integer(grid$source)
means <- fitted_samples(joint, data = grid, family_index = index,
  n_draws = 200, seed = 242)
intervals <- means |>
  group_by(.row) |>
  summarise(estimate = median(.fitted), lower = quantile(.fitted, 0.025),
    upper = quantile(.fitted, 0.975), .groups = "drop")
curves <- bind_cols(grid, intervals |> select(-.row))
ggplot(curves, aes(woodland, estimate)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~ source, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Proportion of woodland", y = "Expected survey response")
```

The first curve estimates detection probability; the second estimates expected
count. These are pointwise intervals for expected responses, not prediction
intervals for future observations. Their shared coefficient draws also retain
uncertainty shared between the two curves. The count response peaks near
intermediate cover, while the logit transform compresses the detection response
between zero and one.

The fitted means can also be checked against mgcv's native prediction. For this
response expression, mgcv needs both columns named in the response expression so it can evaluate the
membership column. The placeholder observation is ignored for the prediction:

```{r native-means}
native_grid <- transform(grid, observed = 0, family_id = index)
head(data.frame(grid, expected = predict(joint, native_grid, type = "response")))
```

To predict actual observations at these cover values, use `simulate()`.
It holds the fitted coefficients and nuisance parameters fixed, then draws
binomial or Poisson responses as appropriate. Coefficient uncertainty is a
separate source of variation: `posterior_samples()` adds that uncertainty.

```{r response-draws}
replicates <- simulate(joint, data = grid, family_index = index,
  nsim = 200, seed = 243)
future <- data.frame(grid, lower = apply(replicates, 1, quantile, 0.025),
  upper = apply(replicates, 1, quantile, 0.975))
future |>
  filter(woodland > 0.49, woodland < 0.51)
```

Even a tightly estimated detection probability yields a future binary response
of zero or one. Counts vary substantially around their fitted mean. The
response families supply this variation; drawing only smooth coefficients
would miss it. Membership is a position in the family list, not an arbitrary
factor code: retain the same mapping when constructing your own prediction data.

## Check each observation process

Raw residual magnitudes are not comparable between binary and count responses.
Probability integral transform (PIT) residuals locate each observation in its
own fitted distribution. At a discrete observation, gratia randomises within
its probability mass; quantile residuals transform those probabilities to
standard-normal scores. See [Model diagnostics](model-checking.html) for the
reference calculations and the distinction from posterior predictive checks.

```{r checks, fig.height=6}
appraise(joint, type = "quantile", by_family = TRUE, seed = 244)
```

Component facets help find a failure confined to one survey. Look for tail
departures in QQ plots, changing residual spread across fitted values, or
disagreement in the observed-versus-fitted panels. Here the component scores
show approximate agreement with their references despite the different scales
of the original responses.

Pooling standard-normal residuals is also possible. The colours retain each
component's identity; histogram densities are calculated separately with
common bin edges. Traditional deviance or response residuals instead default
to separate component facets because their scales differ.

```{r pooled-check}
residuals_hist_plot(joint, type = "quantile", by_family = FALSE, seed = 244)
worm_plot(joint, type = "quantile", by_family = TRUE, seed = 244)
```

A worm plot subtracts the reference quantile, making curvature and departures
near zero easier to see. The separate panels show which observation process
contributes each pattern.

```{r predictive-check}
posterior_predictive_plot(joint, n = 50, seed = 245)
```

The count panel has some departures at individual counts, despite reasonable
overall shape agreement. Its intervals are pointwise and have appreciable
simulation error with 50 replicates; increase that number before judging
individual probability masses closely.

The posterior predictive plot compares separate observed response distributions
with replicated surveys, including approximate coefficient uncertainty. For
these discrete responses the bars describe variation in replicated probability
masses, not intervals on an individual count. A pooled response histogram would
mix probabilities with counts and answer no useful survey question.

## Limits when extending the model

`gfam()` accepts ordinary and extended mgcv families with a scalar response,
including negative binomial, Tweedie, beta, scaled-t and ordered categories.
Gratia response simulation uses each component's fitted parameters and can
simulate ordered-category codes. Response-scale fitted draws for ordinal
components remain unsupported because an ordinal response requires a vector
of category probabilities; link-scale fitted draws are available. General
families with several linear predictors are not `gfam()` components.

Missing required predictors or membership give missing predictions. Missing
responses alone do not prevent prediction. With `na.exclude`, excluded fitting
rows are restored as `NA` in fitted draws and simulations, while checks use the
observations actually fitted. Censored components can simulate latent responses,
but a posterior predictive comparison of censored observations also needs a
censoring mechanism, which is not supplied automatically.

For grouped binomial proportions, supply the number of trials in `weights`;
for Gaussian and Gamma components these weights represent response precision.
Prediction data default to weights of one unless you supply them. These
interpretations differ and should follow the measurement protocol.

Use the component diagnostics to assess the observation distributions and the
separate-curve comparison to decide whether to share the cover response.
Together they address both parts of the model that connect these surveys.
